comparison: Perfect agreement on duration-dependent effects of ischemia (C10-C22). Both evaluations affirm that shorter ischemia causes transient decrease followed by potentiation, while longer ischemia causes sustained failure. OpenEval emphasizes statistical rigor and sample sizes; peer reviewers emphasize the core finding across all three reviewers.

Complete agreement on ECS measurements (C32-C34). Both evaluations accept TMA iontophoresis data as appropriate controls ruling out extracellular space restriction. OpenEval provides detailed methodological validation; peer reviewers note this as part of 'important controls carefully performed.'

Complete agreement on methodological rigor (C91-C113). Both evaluations praise experimental design, data quality, and appropriate controls. OpenEval emphasizes internal consistency and replicability; peer reviewers explicitly state 'exceptional quality' and 'carefully designed.'

Agreement on computational modeling (C43-C46, C114-C116). OpenEval explicitly supports the modeling showing decreased vesicular glutamate cannot explain increased release. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this through general statements about justified conclusions and careful analysis, without specific critique.

Partial disagreement on action potential broadening interpretation (C47-C50, C59-C60). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED while acknowledging speculation about K+ channel inactivation. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, explicitly noting lack of direct experimental demonstration of AP broadening and requesting more direct evidence.

Strong agreement on glutamate uptake resilience (C35-C39, C76 vs C35-C39, C55, C73). Both evaluations affirm that glutamate uptake remains intact after ischemia, demonstrating astrocytic resilience. OpenEval emphasizes decay kinetics analysis and DL-TBOA controls; peer reviewers highlight this as a key finding showing differential vulnerability.

Agreement on iGluSnFR imaging findings (C23-C31 vs C23-C25, C30-C31). Both evaluations support glutamate imaging data showing duration-dependent changes. OpenEval emphasizes systematic controls and transparent reporting of signal loss; peer reviewers highlight the combination of electrophysiology and optical imaging as a strength.

Agreement on hierarchical vulnerability (C51-C55, C12-C14 vs C12-C14, C53-C54, C70). Both evaluations affirm differential vulnerability across synaptic components. OpenEval emphasizes this as a major conceptual advance with converging evidence; peer reviewers highlight astrocytic resilience and comprehensive view of mechanisms.

Strong agreement on increased presynaptic release mechanism (C40-C42, C77-C79 vs C40-C42, C65). Both evaluations affirm γ-DGG competitive antagonism data showing enhanced glutamate release. OpenEval emphasizes statistical significance and validated methodology; peer reviewers confirm this as the primary mechanism underlying potentiation.

Agreement on gradual glutamate recovery observation (C58 vs C58, C51-C52). Both evaluations support the finding that glutamate transients recover despite persistent postsynaptic failure. OpenEval emphasizes value of combined imaging-electrophysiology; peer reviewers affirm bidirectional changes and exceptional data quality.

Agreement on temporal correlation and LTP occlusion (C61-C65 vs C65). Both evaluations accept the temporal correlation analysis linking potentiation to presynaptic mechanisms. OpenEval notes appropriate acknowledgment of limitations; peer reviewers integrate this into overall mechanistic conclusion about presynaptic release.

OpenEval identifies speculation about in vivo PIDs (C74) as UNCERTAIN, appropriately noting this as untested hypothesis for future work. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses this speculative claim about translating findings to periinfarct depolarizations.

OpenEval supports background/context claims (C1-C9) as well-established knowledge with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers do not explicitly evaluate these introductory/background claims, focusing instead on novel experimental findings.

OpenEval supports mechanistic interpretation claims about neuronal depolarization and glutamate/K+ surges (C75, C80-C86). Peer reviewers do not explicitly evaluate these specific mechanistic interpretations, though they accept the overall findings.

OpenEval supports explanation for why PPR analysis was uninformative (C87-C88), citing recent work. Peer reviewers do not explicitly address this methodological limitation or the rationale for alternative approaches.
OpenEval supports acknowledgment of experimental design limitation regarding female mice (C89-C90). Peer reviewers do not explicitly comment on this limitation or sex-specific considerations.

OpenEval supports background claims about glutamate uptake being primarily astrocytic (C66-C67). Peer reviewers do not explicitly evaluate these contextual claims, though they emphasize astrocytic resilience in their overall assessment.

Minimal overlap on astrocytic resilience discussion (C56-C57, C68-C73 vs C70). OpenEval addresses broader claims about lasting effects on uptake being insignificant; peer reviewers focus on overall hierarchical vulnerability. Both agree on astrocytic resilience as a key finding.
